They feature narrow leaves with parallel veins, hollow jointed stems, and fibrous root systems that grow from the base rather than the tip. *Physical Structure* • Stems (Culms): Round and usually hollow between solid joints or nodes. • Leaves: Split into a lower sheath wrapped around the stem and an upper flattened blade. • Roots: Extensive underground fibrous networks that anchor the plant and prevent soil loss. • Growth habit: Grows from the base, allowing survival and rapid recovery after being cut, burned, or grazed. *Types and Habitats* • True grasses (Poaceae): Includes over 10,000 species such as lawn turf, bamboos, and major cereal crops like wheat, rice, and corn. • Grass-like families: Includes sedges (Cyperaceae) and rushes (Juncaceae) which prefer wet or marshy areas. • Global presence: Grasslands cover over 40% of the Earth's land surface, thriving in fields, plains, and varied climates.

fun fact : Mr. Potato Head was invented in 1949 by George Lerner, who designed plastic facial features meant to be pushed into real fruits and vegetables. In 1951, the Hassenfeld brothers (the founders of Hasbro) bought the rights to the toy and officially launched it in 1952. It made history as the first toy ever advertised on television, selling over one million kits in its first year. For those wondering: George Lerner was an American inventor who created the idea for Mr. Potato Head in 1949. He came up with the idea of using plastic facial features that children could stick into real fruits and vegetables to make funny faces. At first, toy companies were not interested because people were concerned about wasting food after World War ii. Eventually, Lerner’s idea was picked up and developed into a toy by Hassenfeld Brothers, the company that later became Hasbro. Mr. Potato Head was officially released in 1952 and became the first toy advertised on television.

For those who don't know: What is grass? Grass consists of low, green, non-woody flowering plants belonging mainly to the true grass family, Poaceae, alongside similar plants like sedges and rushes. They feature narrow leaves with parallel veins, hollow jointed stems, and fibrous root systems that grow from the base rather than the tip. *Physical Structure* • Stems (Culms): Round and usually hollow between solid joints or nodes. • Leaves: Split into a lower sheath wrapped around the stem and an upper flattened blade. • Roots: Extensive underground fibrous networks that anchor the plant and prevent soil loss. • Growth habit: Grows from the base, allowing survival and rapid recovery after being cut, burned, or grazed. *Types and Habitats* • True grasses (Poaceae): Includes over 10,000 species such as lawn turf, bamboos, and major cereal crops like wheat, rice, and corn. • Grass-like families: Includes sedges (Cyperaceae) and rushes (Juncaceae) which prefer wet or marshy areas. • Global presence: Grasslands cover over 40% of the Earth's land surface, thriving in fields, plains, and varied climates.
